trend_source: This TikTok says your education, health, skills and confidence are your greatest asset, so invest in yourself first. It pulled 598.7k views and 170.9k likes, proving the message lands hard.
title: You are your own biggest asset, so insure the income it produces
hooks: Your biggest asset isn't your HDB or your stocks. It's you.
I spend on courses and my health, but I almost forgot to protect the thing paying for all of it.
Invest in yourself first sounds nice until you realise your income has zero backup.
talking_points: Everything the video lists (skills, health, earning potential) runs on one engine: your ability to keep earning.
Investing in yourself grows income; income protection and hospitalisation cover keep that income alive if illness or injury hits.
In Singapore, look at your MediShield Life base and whether an Integrated Shield or income replacement plan fits your situation.
Self-investment and protection are not opposites; one builds the asset, the other insures it.
cta: Comment ASSET and I'll walk you through a simple way to protect the income you're working so hard to grow.
why_it_works: It agrees with a message 170k people already loved, then adds the honest missing piece: the asset needs protecting, not just growing.
how_to_film: Talk straight to camera, point at yourself on the line 'it's you'. Keep energy high for the first 5 seconds, then slow down for the protection point.
author: @dananozime

trend_source: This UK TikTok breaks income into five percentages for essentials, guilt-free spending, savings, debt and investing, earning 562.1k views and 3.2k shares. The formula format clearly travels.
title: The 5-number money split, adapted for a Singapore payslip
hooks: There's a viral money formula going around, but it forgets CPF exists.
Five simple percentages to run your salary, adjusted for how Singaporeans actually get paid.
If you've seen the 60/5/10/10/15 money split, here's what changes once CPF is in the picture.
talking_points: Start from take-home pay after CPF, not gross, so the percentages reflect real cash in hand.
Cap essentials (housing, bills, food, transport), ring-fence a small guilt-free amount, and set targets for short-term savings.
Add a line for any high-interest debt and a consistent monthly amount toward long-term investing.
These are starting benchmarks; adjust to your income and stage, this is not financial advice on specific products.
cta: Save this and try the split on your own numbers, then message me if you want a second pair of eyes.
why_it_works: The percentage-formula format is already proven viral, and localising it for CPF makes it genuinely useful instead of a copy-paste of a UK video.
how_to_film: On-screen text for each number as you say it. First line delivered fast to camera, then hold up fingers for each of the five steps.
author: @maseonomic_

You don't have a money goal problem, you have a 'what it takes' problem.

Peace of mind comes from clearing high-interest debt before chasing returns.

trend_source: This UK TikTok gives quick benchmarks for rent, car value, monthly investing and emergency fund off a salary example, drawing 169k views. The benchmark format is proven.
title: Money benchmarks that actually make sense in Singapore
hooks: A viral rule says your car should cost half your yearly salary. In Singapore, good luck.
Rent, car, emergency fund, investing: here are four benchmarks adjusted for our cost of living.
Foreign money benchmarks fall apart the second you factor in a COE.
talking_points: Housing: keep total housing cost within a comfortable share of take-home so you can still save.
Cars: with COE, the 'half your salary' rule rarely fits; decide if a car is need or reward before stretching.
Emergency fund: aim for several months of expenses in accessible cash before locking money away.
Investing: set a steady monthly amount and automate it; consistency beats big one-off attempts.
cta: Save this list and check how many you're hitting, then DM me which one feels furthest away.
why_it_works: It borrows a proven format but honestly flags that imported benchmarks break under Singapore's COE and housing reality.
how_to_film: Count off four on your fingers with text overlays. Open with the car line for a relatable local laugh.
author: @gray.area.finance

title: The 4 numbers every Singaporean should actually know
hooks: Most people can name their salary but not one of these four numbers.
Financial freedom isn't a vibe, it's four numbers you can work out tonight.

talking_points: Your monthly expenses: the real cost of your life, the base for every other number.
Your emergency buffer: several months of those expenses set aside in cash.
Your freedom number: roughly the invested amount that could cover your expenses long term.
Your monthly investing amount: what you consistently put toward that number, CPF and SRS included.

trend_source: This US reel by @humphreytalks explains four money moves after a Fed rate hike: pay down credit card debt, use higher-yield savings, don't panic on mortgages, keep investing. It reached 414k views, about 11x his usual.
title: Rates moved overseas: 4 calm money moves for Singaporeans
hooks: The Fed just moved rates again, and yes, it can reach your wallet in Singapore.
Before you panic about interest rates, here are four calm moves that actually matter.
Rate headlines are loud; your response should be boring and deliberate.
talking_points: Credit card and floating-rate debt get more expensive first; clearing high-interest balances is one of the strongest moves you can make.
Idle cash shouldn't sit doing nothing; compare where your savings sit and check current rates on official bank sites.
Don't panic-refinance your home loan on a headline; understand what your rate is actually pegged to first.
Keep investing consistently through the noise rather than trying to time the swings.
cta: Ask me one question about how rate moves affect your own plan and I'll answer it.
why_it_works: It rides a genuinely newsy, high-performing explainer while adapting US-specific details into calm, Singapore-relevant actions.
how_to_film: News-desk energy but relaxed. Open with the headline line, then count off four moves with lower-third text. Avoid quoting any specific rate figure.
author: @humphreytalks

hooks: Choosing your retirement over your kid's full uni fund sounds selfish. Hear me out.

title: Reward yourself, but buy the reward on purpose
hooks: You don't need a Conti car. You want one. And that's actually fine.
I waited years before buying a car, and here's the honest reason why.
The problem isn't rewarding yourself; it's rewarding yourself before you can afford it.
talking_points: Separate need from want: a car for real travel demands is different from a status upgrade.
In Singapore, COE and running costs make a car one of the priciest 'rewards' out there.
Reward yourself only after your emergency fund, protection and investing are running.
Different people value different rewards; the discipline is timing it, not skipping it.
